analysis.one_liner: Adds free contraceptive care to Medicare for older and disabled women.
analysis.headline: Introduced December 18, 2025 by four senators from both parties and sent to the Senate Finance Committee, where no vote has been scheduled.
analysis.plain_summary: Medicare today generally does not cover contraception, so women on Medicare — mostly disabled women under 65 and some older women — can pay out of pocket for birth control. This bill would add contraceptive drugs, devices, and related services to Medicare with no deductible or copay, require private Medicare Advantage and Part D drug plans to cover them with no cost-sharing, and order two studies of remaining coverage gaps. It would take effect in 2027.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare beneficiaries who need contraception — chiefly women under 65 who qualify through disability, plus dual Medicare-Medicaid enrollees who would get whichever coverage is stronger. The bill orders an HHS study on covering over-the-counter contraceptives for beneficiaries in traditional Medicare without drug coverage, and GAO studies of gaps in commercial, Medicaid, and TRICARE coverage.

how_it_helps.text: Medicare would cover contraceptive items and services furnished by a physician or practitioner — including counseling, exams, device insertion, ultrasounds, pain management, and follow-up care — with the deductible waived and Medicare paying the full allowed amount, so the beneficiary owes nothing.

Private Medicare Advantage plans could not impose extra cost-sharing on these services, and Part D drug plans would have to cover contraceptive drugs with no deductible, coinsurance, or other cost-sharing starting in plan year 2027.

The Health and Human Services Secretary must ensure that people dually eligible for Medicare and Medicaid get contraceptive coverage at least as comprehensive as their state Medicaid coverage, based on an annual review.

The bill orders a federal study of prescription drug access for Medicare beneficiaries living with disabilities, including oral contraceptives, and studies of which commercial and public plans still do not cover all FDA-approved contraception or waive cost-sharing.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers, through higher Medicare payments for these services, and Part D plan premiums, since plans must cover contraceptive drugs with no cost-sharing. Providers gain a new set of billable services.

drawbacks.text: The bill creates a permanent open-ended Medicare benefit, adding federal spending that taxpayers and Medicare drug-plan premiums would absorb, while the Medicare population is largely past reproductive age; the main direct beneficiaries are a relatively small group of disabled women under 65.

The bill covers these items and services 'regardless of whether such items and services are actually furnished for purposes of contraception,' which broadens the benefit beyond birth control use and increases its cost; over-the-counter contraceptives in traditional Medicare are only studied, not covered.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the women it reaches, the benefit is real and concrete: birth control that currently may be fully out of pocket becomes free. The cost is a modest, permanent addition to federal health spending aimed at a narrow population, and the definitional breadth — covering services whether or not they are for contraception — makes the fiscal size harder to pin down. The studies of remaining gaps in other plans add transparency without cost.

outcome.mechanism: It was just introduced and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, which has not taken any action on it yet.

narrative.text: Senator Hassan introduced the bill on December 18, 2025, joined by Senators Murkowski, Duckworth, and Collins, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance.
Three senators cosponsored the bill after introduction: two Republicans and one Democrat.
The committee has taken no further action, and the bill has not received a hearing, markup, or floor vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one has won or lost yet. If the bill stalls in committee, the current arrangement continues: Medicare beneficiaries who need contraception keep paying out of pocket, and Medicare pays nothing for these services.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was introduced by two Democrats and two Republicans together, and its three follow-on cosponsors split two Republicans and one Democrat; no senator has opposed it on the record.

industries.industry: Health insurers (Medicare Advantage and Part D plans)
industries.note: Insurers must cover contraceptive drugs and services with no cost-sharing starting in 2027, an added cost to their plans, though they remain the delivery channel and the government adjusts payments to plans. Their interest in avoiding a new required benefit runs against the beneficiary's interest in free coverage.
Contraceptive counseling, procedures, and device care become billable Medicare services paid at 100 percent of the allowed amount, expanding revenue for the providers who serve these patients.
Contraceptive drugs become a covered Part D category with no patient cost-sharing, creating a guaranteed paying market, though it is a modest segment compared to the drug industry overall.

analysis.trajectory: With only three cosponsors and a referral to the Senate Finance Committee in mid-December, the odds of standalone action are low; the bill most likely sits unless it is folded into a broader Medicare or health package, since Finance historically moves most Medicare benefit changes through larger vehicles.
